title: 📘 UNIT 3: SOCIAL, ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL DEVELOPMENTS IN ETHIOPIA, MID-19TH C. TO 1941
3.1 🐪 Long-Distance Trade and People's Interaction
notes:
Long-distance trade → movement of commodities between distant regions through caravan routes and market centers.

Factors for revival:

• Rise of the five Oromo kingdoms in the Gibe region.

• Reappearance of northern merchants in southwestern Ethiopia.

• Improvement of political conditions along the Red Sea and Arabia.

• Greater security and importance of Red Sea trade.

Major commodities:
• Ivory.
• Gold.
• Civet.
• Wax.
• Animal skins.
• Coffee.
• Slaves.

Major merchants:
• Jabarti → mainly Muslim merchants from northern Ethiopia.

• Afkala → dominant Muslim merchants in southwestern Ethiopia.

📌 Trade encouraged movement of people, exchange of ideas and cultures, and interaction between northern and southwestern Ethiopia.

title: 3.1.1 🗺️ Trade Routes and Market Centers
notes:
Major routes included:
• Bonga–Jimma–Saka–Assendabo–Basso–Gondar → Sudan or Massawa.

• Bonga–Jimma–Saka–Assendabo–Aussa–Tajura/Obock.

• Bonga–Jimma–Soddo–Ankober–Harar–Zeila/Berbera.

Important market centers:
• Assendabo.
• Basso.
• Gondar.
• Ankober.
• Bati and Ancharo.
• Soddo.
• Harar.

📌 Basso connected merchants from Tigray, Gondar, Wollo, Shewa and southern regions.

title: 3.1.2 🤝 Trade as a Factor for People's Interaction
notes:
Long-distance trade:
• Connected northern and southwestern Ethiopia.
• Increased interaction among different peoples.
• Encouraged cultural and intellectual exchange.
• Helped spread Islam into the Gibe region through Muslim merchants.
• Strengthened some southwestern rulers and their state institutions.
• Facilitated the growth of trade and political relationships.

title: 3.2 👑 Power Rivalry and Consolidating Central Government (1855–1913)
notes:
Zemene Mesafint → Era of Princes, approximately 1769–1855.

Characteristics:
• Weakening of Solomonic kings.
• Strong regional rulers and rivalries.
• Frequent civil wars.
• Regional political division.
• Religious doctrinal controversies.
• Heavy burdens on peasants.

Yejju Rases dominated Ethiopian politics from 1769 to 1855 and used Debre Tabor as their major political center.

title: 3.2.1 ⚔️ Emperor Tewodros II
notes:
Kassa Hailu → became Emperor Tewodros II in 1855.

Major aims:
• End the Zemene Mesafint.
• Centralize political authority.
• Reunify Ethiopia.
• Establish a stronger national army.
• Reduce the power of regional rulers.
• Reform the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.
• Modernize the country and obtain modern weapons.

📌 Tewodros laid important foundations for modern Ethiopian state formation.

title: 3.2.2 🏰 Tewodros II and Britain
notes:
Tewodros sought British technological assistance for modernization.

Conflict developed after Britain failed to provide the assistance he expected and Tewodros detained British representatives and other Europeans.

1868 → British expedition to Ethiopia.

Meqdela → British forces stormed and plundered the fortress after defeating Tewodros's forces.

📌 Tewodros died at Meqdela in 1868, but the process of ending regionalism and strengthening central government continued.

title: 3.2.3 🛡️ Emperor Yohannis IV
notes:
Yohannis IV continued the process of consolidating Ethiopia while giving considerable autonomy to regional rulers who recognized his authority and paid tribute.

Major features:
• Allowed regional rulers internal autonomy.
• Fought Egyptian aggression.
• Resisted Italian expansion from Massawa.
• Fought the Mahdists in Sudan.
• Attempted religious uniformity.

1889 → Yohannis IV was fatally wounded at the Battle of Metemma while fighting the Mahdists.

📌 His death contributed to the shift of political power from the north to Shewa.

title: 3.2.4 👑 Menilek II and the Shift to Shewa
notes:
Menilek of Shewa succeeded Yohannis IV and became Emperor Menilek II in 1889.

Major features of his rule:
• Continued centralization and state formation.
• Expanded the territory of the Shewan kingdom.
• Strengthened military power.
• Controlled important trade areas.
• Defended Ethiopia against colonial aggression.
• Continued modernization.
• Achieved victory over Italy at Adwa in 1896.

📌 The political center shifted from the northern regions to Shewa.

title: 3.3 🗺️ Territorial Expansion and Incorporation of Kingdoms
notes:
Menilek's territorial expansion occurred in three major phases:
• 1870–1889.
• 1889–1896.
• 1896–1900.

Main reasons:
• Control of fertile lands and natural resources.
• Control of long-distance trade.
• Expansion of political authority.
• Strengthening and unification of the Ethiopian state.
• Access to commodities such as ivory, gold, civet, coffee and slaves.

title: 3.3.1 ⚔️ Resistance and Incorporation
notes:
Different peoples responded differently to Menilek's expansion.

• Some regions submitted peacefully.
• Others offered strong military resistance.
• Southern Gurage resisted under Hassan Enjamo.
• Arsi Oromo resisted strongly and were defeated at Azule in 1886.
• Gibe and Leqa states included areas that submitted peacefully.

📌 Menilek's expansion involved both military conquest and negotiated submission.

title: 3.3.2 🌾 Land Tenure and the Gebbar–Melkegna System
notes:
Gult → land rights granted by the state to officials or institutions.

Melkegna → holder of gult rights who represented the government in the area.

Gebbar → peasant required to provide taxes and services to the landholder/state.

Services included:
• Agricultural labor.
• Construction.
• Transportation.
• Guarding prisoners.
• Domestic services.

📌 Gult rights gradually became hereditary, contributing to the development of the rist-gult system.

title: 3.3.3 📐 Qelad System and Southern Land Tenure
notes:
Qelad → land-measurement and taxation system introduced in newly incorporated southern regions.

Effects:
• Increased state revenue.
• Facilitated land appropriation and privatization.
• Reduced the security of many peasants over their land.
• Turned some land-owning farmers into insecure tenants.
• Forced some displaced or landless peasants to migrate to towns in search of work.

title: 3.4 🌍 External Relations, Challenges and Threats
notes:
Major external challenges included:
• British expedition against Tewodros II.
• Egyptian aggression.
• Mahdist threat.
• Italian colonial expansion.
• French and Italian competition in the Horn of Africa.

Ethiopian resistance relied on military mobilization, political diplomacy and defense of territorial independence.

title: 3.4.1 ⚔️ Battles of Gundet and Gura
notes:
Egyptian ruler Khedive Ismael Pasha launched aggression against Ethiopia in the 1870s.

Battle of Gundet → 16 November 1875.
• Ethiopian forces under Yohannis IV defeated the Egyptian army.

Battle of Gura → 7–9 March 1876.
• Ethiopian forces again defeated the larger Egyptian army.
• Large quantities of Egyptian weapons were captured.

📌 The victories strengthened Ethiopia's resistance to Egyptian expansion.

title: 3.4.2 🇫🇷🇮🇹 Foreign Powers in the Horn of Africa
notes:
European powers established colonial possessions around Ethiopia:

🇮🇹 Italy → Eritrea and Italian Somaliland.
🇫🇷 France → Djibouti/French Somaliland.
🇬🇧 Britain → territories around Sudan and British Somaliland.

📌 European colonial expansion increased the external pressure on Ethiopia and made diplomatic relations increasingly important.

title: 3.5 🏆 The Victory of Adwa (1896)
notes:
Treaty of Wuchale → signed between Menilek II and Italy on 2 May 1889.

Article 17 had different meanings in the Amharic and Italian versions.

Amharic version → Ethiopia could use Italian assistance in foreign relations if desired.

Italian version → Ethiopia was required to conduct foreign relations through Italy, implying a protectorate.

📌 The disagreement over Article 17 became a major cause of the conflict between Ethiopia and Italy.

title: 3.5.1 ⚔️ Battle of Adwa
notes:
Date → 1 March 1896.

Ethiopian forces → about 100,000 troops, with nearly three-quarters equipped with modern rifles.

Important factors:
• Large-scale mobilization.
• Ethiopian unity.
• Strong leadership.
• Knowledge of the terrain.
• Intelligence gained from defections from the Italian side.
• Italian strategic mistakes and poor coordination.

Result → decisive Ethiopian victory.

26 October 1896 → Treaty of Addis Ababa annulled the Treaty of Wuchale and Italy officially recognized Ethiopia's independence while retaining Eritrea.

title: 3.5.2 🌍 Significance of Adwa
notes:
🇪🇹 National significance:
• Preserved Ethiopia's political independence.
• Strengthened national unity and pride.
• Contributed to internationally recognized boundaries.

🌍 International significance:
• Became a symbol of African resistance to colonialism.
• Challenged the idea of European racial superiority.
• Inspired Pan-Africanism, Ethiopianism and Rastafarianism.
• Encouraged anti-colonial and anti-imperialist movements.

title: 3.6 ⛪ Religious Doctrinal Controversies and Reforms
notes:
Major Ethiopian Orthodox doctrinal debates included:

• Tewahedo → Union.
• Qebat → Unction.
• Ye Tsega Lej → Grace.
• Hulet Ledet/Karra → two births of Christ.
• Soset Ledet → three births of Christ.

These controversies often had regional characteristics and weakened the unifying role of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.

title: 3.6.1 🕊️ Yohannis IV's Religious Reform
notes:
Council of Boru Meda (1878) → Yohannis IV attempted to establish religious uniformity.

Wollo Muslims were given the choice of:
• Conversion to Orthodox Christianity, or
• Loss of land and property.

Some converted while others resisted.

Yohannis IV also ordered Orthodox Christians to follow the Tewahedo doctrine in an attempt to end doctrinal disputes within the Church.

title: 3.6.2 🇪🇷 Birth of Eritrea as an Italian Colony
notes:
1879 → Italian Rubatino Shipping Company purchased Assab from the local Afar Sultan.

1882 → Assab transferred to the Italian government.

1883 → Treaty of Commerce and Friendship between Menilek and Italy.

1887 → Convention of Neutrality.

2 May 1889 → Treaty of Wuchale.

1 January 1890 → Italy declared the creation of the colony of Eritrea.

📌 Italy gradually expanded from Assab and the Mereb Melash region toward the Mereb River.

title: 3.7 👑 Power Struggle among Ruling Elites (1906–1935)
notes:
1906 → Menilek II suffered his first major stroke and Ras Mekonnen died.

Succession became a major political issue.

1906 → Britain, France and Italy signed the Tripartite Treaty concerning their interests in the Horn of Africa.

1907 → Menilek established Ethiopia's first Council of Ministers.

1909 → Lej Iyasu was officially designated successor, with Ras Tesema Nadew as regent.

📌 Political rivalry intensified around the imperial succession.

title: 3.7.1 👑 Lej Iyasu and Empress Zewditu
notes:
Lej Iyasu → designated successor of Menilek II.

Etege Taytu → gained strong political influence and opposed aspects of the succession arrangement.

1910 → Taytu was removed from the imperial court after opposition from Shewan nobles.

1913 → Menilek II died.

Lej Iyasu became emperor but was later deposed in 1916.

Zewditu → became Empress after Iyasu's deposition.

Ras Teferi Mekonnen → became heir and king, gaining increasing political influence.

title: 3.7.2 👑 Rise of Haile Selassie I
notes:
1930 → Ras Teferi defeated Ras Gugsa Wole at the Battle of Anchim.

Zewditu died shortly afterward.

2 November 1930 → Ras Teferi was crowned Emperor Haile Selassie I.

1931 Constitution → strengthened imperial authority and reduced the power of hereditary rulers.

1930 → Imperial Bodyguard established with Belgian assistance.

1934 → Holeta Military Academy established.

📌 Centralization and modernization continued until the Italian invasion of 1935.

title: 3.8 🇮🇹 Italian Aggression and Patriotic Resistance
notes:
Causes of the 1935 Italian invasion:
• Italian desire for revenge after Adwa.
• Mussolini's Fascist expansionism.
• Desire to build a new Italian empire.
• Colonial ambitions in Africa.
• Strategic and political interests.

3 October 1935 → Italy invaded Ethiopia from Eritrea.

Major Ethiopian commanders included:
• Ras Kassa Hailu.
• Ras Seyoum Mengesha.
• Ras Mulugeta Yigezu.
• Ras Emeru Haile Selassie.

📌 Ethiopian forces fought strongly but suffered from weaker coordination, weapons and air power.

title: 3.8.1 ⚔️ Major Battles and Occupation
notes:
Major events:
• Tembien battles → January and February 1936.
• Amba Aradom → Ethiopian defeat under Ras Mulugeta.
• Maychew → 31 March 1936; final major battle on the northern front.
• 5 May 1936 → Italian forces captured Addis Ababa.

Italian military advantages:
• Air superiority.
• Better weapons.
• Larger military resources.
• Better coordination.

📌 Italy occupied Ethiopia, but nationwide patriotic resistance continued.

title: 3.8.2 🕊️ League of Nations and Italian Occupation
notes:
Ethiopia joined the League of Nations in 1923.

Haile Selassie appealed to the League of Nations for assistance against Italy.

League response → sanctions were imposed on both Ethiopia and Italy, which failed to stop Italian aggression.

1937 → assassination attempt against Graziani was followed by a large-scale massacre in Addis Ababa and surrounding areas.

1936–1941 → Italian occupation continued while patriotic resistance remained active.

1941 → Italian forces were finally defeated and expelled.

notes:
